# Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga Pācittiya 20 (Bu-Vb Pc20)

**ID:** Bu-Vb Pc20  
**Section:** Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga (bu-vb)  
**Collection:** Vinaya  
**Title (Pali):** Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga Pācittiya 20  
**Title (English, from literature):** Pouring water with living beings in it  
**tipitaka.org (CST):** [https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/vin02m1.mul0.xml](https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/vin02m1.mul0.xml)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Sappāṇaka Sutta* (Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga Pācittiya 20) formulates the monastic rule prohibiting a Buddhist monk from pouring or sprinkling water containing living beings onto grass or clay [Harvey; Schmithausen 1991]. A monk who knowingly does so must confess the offense. Analyzing culpability in the Vinaya, Peter Harvey observes that while inadvertence or ignorance that the water contains life incurs no offense, acting when one suspects or is unsure whether the water contains living beings constitutes a minor offense of wrongdoing (*dukkaṭa*), demonstrating that foresight or suspicion without direct killing intent carries culpability [Harvey]. Lambert Schmithausen notes that Pācittiya 20 and Pācittiya 62 (which forbids drinking water containing living beings) represent borderline cases under the broader precept against taking animal life, where the term *pāṇa* or *pāṇaka* specifically designates tiny animals or organisms [Schmithausen 1991; Bechert 1992]. In contemporary practice, monastic observance of this rule has included scrupulous inspection of water buckets before use to ensure no tiny creatures are harmed [Dhammika].

 An English translation of the text has been made by Bhikkhu Brahmali.
